slides.say: A phone game starts with two large bubbles on the screen. Popping a large bubble splits it into five small bubbles. Popping a small bubble makes it disappear. After exactly three pops, how many bubbles can be on the screen?

So they don't ask how many there must be. They ask what can be. One road that really happens and ends on a choice is enough. Nothing tells us which bubble to pop first, so this is a general problem. [short pause] We'll solve it in two different ways, by trial and error, and then with an insight.
[short pause] Let's start with trial and error. We try one road of pops and follow the game. At the start there are two large bubbles, and no small ones.

Pop one. There are no small bubbles yet, so the first pop has to hit a large one. That large bubble is gone, and five small ones appear. So we have one large and five small. One plus five is six bubbles. Six is in the choices, but that's after one pop only, so we keep going.

Now the road splits, because we can pop the large one or a small one. Let's take one road, and pop the other large bubble. It turns into five more small ones. So there are no large ones left, and five plus five is ten small ones. Ten is a choice too, but that's after two pops. The question says exactly three pops.
Pop three. Only small bubbles are left, so we pop a small one, and it disappears. Ten minus one is nine bubbles.
Nine is in the choices. They ask what can be, and this road really happens. So there can be nine bubbles, and choice number three is our answer. This time we were lucky on the first road.
at: choice number three is our answer

slides.say: What if we had taken the other road? Let's see it, because in another question the first road can miss. The first pop is the same, one large and five small.
at: The first pop is the same

slides.say: This time, pop two hits a small bubble, and it disappears. One of the five small ones is gone, so four small are left. So we have one large and four small, five bubbles.
at: One of the five small ones

slides.say: Pop three can go two ways. If we pop the large one, it turns into five small ones. Four plus five is nine small bubbles, nine again.
at: If we pop the large one

slides.say: If we pop a small one, one large and three small are left, four bubbles. Four is not in the choices. If this had been our first road, we'd just try again. That's trial and error. We try, we miss, and we try again.
at: If we pop a small one

slides.say: So every road ends at nine or at four, and only nine is in the choices. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now the insight. Instead of following the bubbles, let's look at what one pop changes. A large pop takes away one bubble and adds five. Minus one plus five is plus four.
A small pop just takes one bubble away, so it's minus one.
There are only two large bubbles, and the first pop must be large. Say two pops are large and one is small. We start at two. Two plus four is six. Six plus four is ten. And ten minus one is nine.

Say only one pop is large. Two plus four is six, and then two small pops take away two. Six minus two is four. That's the four we found before. So the totals are nine and four, and only nine is in the choices. Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Say only one pop is large
only nine is in the choices
